children: By Staff Writer

AMMAN — Aqaba’s date palm sector is emerging as a promising driver of agricultural growth and economic diversification in southern Jordan, with expanding orchards creating opportunities for food processing, investment and domestic and international marketing.

Cultivated date palm areas in Aqaba Governorate now cover about 10,377 dunums, with approximately 98,630 palm trees, including 86,181 female trees, according to data from the Aqaba Directorate of Agriculture. Registered farms produced about 790 tonnes of dates in 2025, with production concentrated in Quwayra, Wadi Araba and Aqaba.
Thaer Rawajfeh, director of agriculture in Aqaba, has recently told the Jordan News Agency, Petra, that the figures provide a strong production and investment base for developing the sector.
He said, however, that current production figures do not fully reflect the sector’s potential, as large areas have been planted with young trees that have yet to reach commercial production.

Rawajfeh said that the expansion in cultivated land and the growing number of registered palm trees present an opportunity to increase production and strengthen the competitiveness of Aqaba’s dates in local and international markets.
Quwayra currently accounts for the largest share of recorded production.
The desert region’s registered farms produced about 545 tonnes in 2025, or nearly 69 per cent of the southern governorate’s total registered output.
The area cultivated with date palms in Quwayra stands at about 2,085 dunums, containing approximately 28,280 trees.
The area has a diverse range of varieties, with Barhi among the most prominent. Farm sizes vary widely, from small holdings of less than 10 dunums to large estates covering hundreds of dunums.
Wadi Araba has the largest cultivated area, covering about 7,200 dunums and containing approximately 64,550 palm trees. Yet its registered farms produced about 195 tonnes in 2025.
Rawajfeh said the disparity between cultivated area and production is largely linked to the age of the trees and the stage of development of individual farms.
Some trees are only two or three years old and have not yet entered commercial production, while others are as old as 32 years and are already producing substantial yields.
The age profile of the orchards, he said, points to the possibility of a significant increase in production in the coming years as younger trees reach full fruiting capacity.
Within Aqaba city, date palm cultivation covers about 1,092 dunums, with roughly 5,800 trees. Registered farms in the area produced approximately 50 tonnes in 2025.
Production remains uneven across farms.

According to the directorate’s records, one farm produced about 200 tonnes, while others recorded yields of 100, 70 and 50 tonnes. Some newer farms recorded no production during the season because their trees had not yet reached productive maturity.

The Barhi variety remains one of the principal varieties cultivated in Quwayra and WadiAraba, alongside several other types. Some records, however, continue to classify varieties as “unknown”, highlighting the need for continued updating and documentation of agricultural data.

Rawajfeh said Quwayra’s current production lead is expected to remain important, but WadiAraba’s larger cultivated area and significant number of young trees could enable it to assume a greater role in the governorate’s future date production.

With established orchards expanding alongside thousands of younger trees approaching commercial maturity, Aqaba’s date palm sector is gradually moving beyond traditional agriculture toward a broader economic activity involving production, processing, investment and marketing.
This article was first published in Al Rai newspaper.
